01What's covered

What we fix.

It gets dunked in salt water every trip, then forgotten about. We don't forget about it. The numbers match the drawing above.

  1. 1

    Wheel bearings & seals

    Bearings cleaned, inspected and repacked or replaced, with new seals to keep the salt water out.

  2. 2

    Brakes, calipers & cables

    Seized calipers, worn pads, corroded discs and stretched cables put right, so the trailer pulls up straight.

  3. 3

    LED light conversions

    Sealed, submersible LED lights in place of bulbs that fail every second trip.

  4. 4

    Trailer rewires

    New cable run properly along the frame, with sealed joins and a plug that makes good contact.

  5. 5

    Rollers, skids & bunks

    Flat-spotted rollers and worn skids replaced and set up to suit the hull, so the boat loads straight and sits right.

  6. 6

    Winches, straps & chains

    Winch, strap and safety chain checked and replaced before they let go on the ramp.

  7. 7

    Couplings & jockey wheels

    Worn couplings and seized jockey wheels replaced, so hitching up is quick and stays secure.

  8. 8

    Springs, axles & hubs

    Rusted springs, bent axles and worn hubs replaced before they leave you on the side of the road.

02Inside the hub

Where the salt gets in.

Wheel bearings are the most common reason a boat trailer ends up on the side of the road. This is what is inside each hub, and the one part that keeps the water out.

Swipe sideways to see the whole hub →

  • /01

    Hot hub, cold water

    A hub is warm after a tow. Back it into the water and it cools quickly, which draws water in past the seal.

  • /02

    Water turns grease to paste

    Once salt water is inside, the grease breaks down and the bearing starts to pit and rust.

  • /03

    A seal is cheap. A hub is not

    New seals at each service keep the water out. Left alone, a failed bearing can take the hub and the axle with it.

Early warnings

  • 01A hub that is hot to touch after a tow
  • 02Grease flung on the inside of the wheel or guard
  • 03Rumbling or grinding from a wheel
  • 04Brakes that drag, grab or do nothing
  • 05Lights that fail after every launch
  • 06The boat sits crooked, or is hard to winch on

04Good to know

Trailer questions.

Can't see yours here? Ask it in the booking form or give us a call.

How often should boat trailer bearings be serviced?

As a rule of thumb, once a year for a trailer that goes in salt water, and sooner if a seal has let water in. A warm hub, grease on the wheel or any rumbling means it needs looking at now, not at the next service.

Does the boat have to come off the trailer?

For most jobs, no. Bearings, brakes, lights and couplings can be done with the boat on. Roller and bunk work can need the boat off, and we will tell you when you book.

My trailer lights keep failing. Is it the lights or the wiring?

Often both. Bulb-type lights let water in and corrode, and old joins along the frame break down in salt. We test what is there first and quote from that. A sealed LED set and a proper rewire is usually the lasting fix.

Can you look at the trailer while the boat is booked in for something else?

Yes. It usually makes sense to check bearings, brakes and lights in the same booking as a service or an install.
